## Plotly

This lecture will be based on the information that is available on the *plotly* website <https://plotly.com/r/getting-started/>

### Installation

First, we need to install plotly

```{r}
#install.packages("plotly")
```

The very basic plot

```{r}
library(plotly)
fig <- plot_ly(midwest, x = ~percollege, color = ~state, type = "box")
fig
```

We can check what type of data is required to get this graph

```{r}
head(midwest)
```

### Graphical components

Unlike *ggplot* and its grammar of graphs approach, *plotly* has a core figure data structure referred to as **charts**. They are automatically-generated from the *machine-readable Plotly.js schema reference*. This means, that the whole structure of a graph is set as a *json* file that is highly adaptable and only specific attributes differentiate one graph from another.

### Plotly attributes

Every chart needs to specify the parts that are needed to produce the desired output. The graph description has two categories

1.  Traces. It describes a single series of data in a graph
2.  Layout. It applies to the rest of the charts characteristics as *annotations*, *tittle*, etc.

```{r}
   p <- plot_ly(economics,
                 type = "scatter",        # all "scatter" attributes: https://plotly.com/r/reference/#scatter
                 x = ~date,               # more about scatter's "x": /r/reference/#scatter-x
                 y = ~uempmed,            # more about scatter's "y": /r/reference/#scatter-y
                 name = "unemployment",   # more about scatter's "name": /r/reference/#scatter-name
                 marker = list(           # marker is a named list, valid keys: /r/reference/#scatter-marker
                   color="#264E86"        # more about marker's "color" attribute: /r/reference/#scatter-marker-color
                 )) %>%

      add_trace(x = ~date,                                         # scatter's "x": /r/reference/#scatter-x
                y = ~fitted((loess(uempmed ~ as.numeric(date)))),  # scatter's "y": /r/reference/#scatter-y
                mode = 'lines',                                    # scatter's "y": /r/reference/#scatter-mode
                line = list(                                       # line is a named list, valid keys: /r/reference/#scatter-line
                  color = "#5E88FC",                               # line's "color": /r/reference/#scatter-line-color
                  dash = "dashed"                                  # line's "dash" property: /r/reference/#scatter-line-dash
                )
      ) %>%

      layout(                        # all of layout's properties: /r/reference/#layout
             title = "Unemployment", # layout's title: /r/reference/#layout-title
             xaxis = list(           # layout's xaxis is a named list. List of valid keys: /r/reference/#layout-xaxis
                title = "Time",      # xaxis's title: /r/reference/#layout-xaxis-title
                showgrid = F),       # xaxis's showgrid: /r/reference/#layout-xaxis-showgrid
             yaxis = list(           # layout's yaxis is a named list. List of valid keys: /r/reference/#layout-yaxis
                title = "uidx")     # yaxis's title: /r/reference/#layout-yaxis-title
      )
   
```

Then, we can call the graphical object

```{r}
p
```

The whole construction is more intimidating, as there are many more attributes to tweak.

## EDA

We will conduct some basic EDA in plotly. First, we load our data set

```{r}
library(DAAG)
fossum <-subset(possum,sex=="f")
attach(fossum)
```

Next, plotly will take care of this

```{r}
pl.fig<-plot_ly(x= ~ totlngth, type="histogram")
pl.fig
```

```{r}
pl.fig1<-plot_ly(x= ~ totlngth, type="histogram",nbinsx=50)
pl.fig1
```

We can also change more on the histogram

```{r}
pl.fig2<-plot_ly(x= ~ totlngth, type="histogram",histnorm="probability density")
pl.fig2
```

We can get a better result with the combination of *plotly* and *ggplot2*

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
gg<-ggplot(fossum, aes(totlngth, color="density"))+
  geom_histogram(aes(y=after_stat(density)),bins=30,fill="#67B7D1",alpha=0.5)+
  geom_density(color="#67B7D1")+
  geom_rug(color="#67B7D1")+
  ylab("")+
  xlab("")+
  theme(legend.title=element_blank())+
  scale_color_manual(values=c("density"="#67B7D1"))

ggplotly(gg) %>%  
 layout(plot_bgcolor='#e5ecf6',   
             xaxis = list(   
               title='Tooth Length', 
               zerolinecolor = '#ffff',   
               zerolinewidth = 2,   
               gridcolor = 'ffff'),   
             yaxis = list(   
               title='Density', 
               zerolinecolor = '#ffff',   
               zerolinewidth = 2,   
               gridcolor = 'ffff')) 

```

We will extend this plot to accommodate different levels given by the variable *Pop* as we did before

```{r}
plp1<-ggplot(fossum, aes(totlngth,fill=Pop))+
  geom_histogram(bindwidth=2.5)+
  geom_rug(sides="t",length = unit(0.3,"cm"))
fig<- ggplotly(plp1)
fig
```

Or even more sophisticated

```{r}
plp2<-ggplot(data=fossum)+
  geom_histogram(aes(x=totlngth,y=after_stat(density),fill=Pop),bins=30,alpha=0.7)+
  geom_density(aes(x=totlngth,color=Pop))+
  labs(title = "Female Opposum Data", subtitle = "Fist Investigation") +xlab("Total Length (cm)") + ylab("Frequency")+labs(caption = "BMIG 5211 experiment")
  
ggplotly(plp2)%>% 
  layout(plot_bgcolor='#e5ecf6',   
             xaxis = list(   
               title='Total Length (cm)', 
               zerolinecolor = '#ffff',   
               zerolinewidth = 2,   
               gridcolor = 'ffff'),   
             yaxis = list(   
               title="Frequency", 
               zerolinecolor = '#ffff',   
               zerolinewidth = 2,   
               gridcolor = 'ffff')) 

```

For more information <https://plotly.com/r/distplot/>

## Boxplots

Once again, we will use a basic example and expand upon it.

```{r}
fig <- plot_ly(y = ~totlngth, type = "box",name="Tooth length")
fig
```

Or if we want to use the level *pop* to differentiate

```{r}
fossum.vic<-fossum[fossum$Pop=="Vic",]
fossum.nvic<-fossum[fossum$Pop != "Vic",]
y1<-fossum.vic$footlgth
y2<-fossum.nvic$footlgth
fig <-plot_ly(y=y1, type="box",name="Victoria")
fig <-fig %>% add_trace(y=y2,name="Elsewhere")
fig
```

And if we want it horizontal

```{r}
fig <-plot_ly(x=y1, type="box",name="Victoria")
fig <-fig %>% add_trace(x=y2,name="Elsewhere")
fig
```

## Patterns in bivariate data

In this part we will use the electrical resistance example.

```{r}
p<-ggplot(fruitohms, aes(juice,ohms))+geom_point()+
  stat_smooth(method="lm", col="blue")
ggplotly(p)
```

Or we can use loess the same way we did

```{r}
p1<-ggplot(fruitohms, aes(juice,ohms))+geom_point()+
  stat_smooth(method =NULL , col="blue")
p2<-ggplotly(p1)
p2
```
